alternative_explanations: Collections have slowed because credit control weakened, not because sales are bad.
Credit terms were deliberately extended to win the extra sales.
A few large credit sales near the period-end distort the receivables figure.
Revenue recognition timing differences rather than a real collection problem.
info_needed: Aged receivables listing and collection history
Current credit terms vs prior period terms
Cash flow statement (operating cash flow vs profit)
Receivable days trend over several periods
Any changes in customer mix or key customer payment behaviour
interpretation: Sales growth is not converting into cash. Receivables are absorbing the cash the business needs to operate, which is a classic early sign of working-capital strain even while the profit figure looks healthy.
recommended_analysis: Receivable days and cash conversion cycle
Operating cash flow vs profit reconciliation
Aged debt review and provision adequacy
required_conditions: Applies when sales are growing but the cash position is deteriorating and receivables are growing faster than sales.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — working-capital theory
title: Working-capital pressure: revenue up, cash down, receivables rising faster than sales

alternative_explanations: A temporary demand spike rather than a sustained trend.
Inefficient scheduling or poor planning, not true capacity shortage.
A labour or skills shortage rather than physical capacity.
An upstream supply bottleneck masquerading as internal capacity.
info_needed: Capacity utilisation by bottleneck resource
Demand forecast and order backlog
Cost and lead time of capacity expansion options
Feasibility and cost of outsourcing or overtime
Customer tolerance for delays and cancellation risk
interpretation: The business cannot meet demand with current capacity. Every delayed order risks lost sales and damaged customer relationships, so this is both an operational and a strategic decision point.
recommended_analysis: Relevant-cost comparison of expand vs outsource vs overtime
required_conditions: Applies when demand is growing, utilisation is at or above 90%, and delivery delays are occurring.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — capacity planning / theory of constraints
title: Capacity constraint: demand rising, utilisation near full, orders delayed

alternative_explanations: A deliberate low-margin strategy to gain market share or clear stock.
A shift in sales mix towards lower-margin products.
One-off costs (e.g. redundancy, write-downs) depressing the margin temporarily.
Changes in cost allocation or accounting policy rather than economics.
info_needed: Selling price and input cost trends by product
Sales mix changes over the period
Competitor pricing behaviour
Breakdown of cost of sales into material, labour and overhead
interpretation: The business keeps less from each unit of sales. Either selling prices are under pressure or input costs are rising faster than prices can be increased.
recommended_analysis: Margin bridge (price vs cost vs mix effects)
required_conditions: Applies when gross margin is falling over successive periods.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — cost-volume-profit analysis
title: Declining margins: gross margin trending down

alternative_explanations: New borrowing funds value-creating investment, not distress.
Equity was eroded by losses or dividends rather than debt rising.
A revaluation or accounting change moved the ratio.
Debt was drawn temporarily against a confirmed future inflow.
info_needed: Purpose and terms of new borrowing
Debt maturity profile and covenant headroom
Interest cover trend
Forecast cash flows available for debt service
interpretation: Financial risk is increasing: a larger share of capital is debt, so fixed interest obligations grow and the margin for error in a downturn shrinks.
recommended_analysis: Debt maturity and refinancing risk review
required_conditions: Applies when the gearing ratio is rising over successive periods.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — capital structure theory
title: Rising gearing: debt burden increasing

alternative_explanations: Deliberate bulk buying to secure discounts or beat expected price rises.
Stock-building ahead of a seasonal peak or confirmed large order.
Supply-chain precaution after past disruptions.
A change in product mix towards items that legitimately need more stock.
info_needed: Inventory ageing and slow-moving/obsolete stock report
Net realisable value testing
Purchasing policy and order quantities
Sales forecasts vs stock cover
interpretation: More cash is locked in stock and it is turning over more slowly. This absorbs working capital and raises the risk of obsolescence and write-downs.
recommended_analysis: Inventory days trend and ageing analysis
required_conditions: Applies when inventory balances are rising and inventory days are lengthening.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — inventory management theory
title: Inventory build-up: stock rising and inventory days lengthening

alternative_explanations: The budget itself was unrealistic or based on bad assumptions.
General price inflation moved costs, not inefficiency.
A volume change distorts fixed-cost comparisons (use a flexed budget).
One-off events outside management's control.
info_needed: Flexed budget for the actual activity level
Price vs usage/efficiency split of each material variance
Responsibility-centre breakdown
Budget-setting assumptions and process
interpretation: Performance is off-plan. The variance must be split into price, usage/efficiency and volume effects to find what management can actually control.
required_conditions: Applies when actual results are materially adverse to budget.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — standard costing / variance analysis theory
title: Adverse budget variances: actuals materially worse than budget

alternative_explanations: Cash flows are understated (e.g. follow-on opportunities omitted).
The discount rate is set too high for the project's risk.
Real-option value (expand, abandon, defer) is ignored in the NPV.
The strategic benefit is real but smaller than claimed.
info_needed: Itemised strategic benefits with quantification attempts
Sensitivity of NPV to key assumptions
Real options embedded in the project
Opportunity cost of the capital committed
interpretation: On pure financial grounds the project destroys value. Strategic benefits must be specific, quantified where possible, and weighed explicitly -- 'strategic' must not become a vague excuse for a bad project.
recommended_analysis: Sensitivity and scenario analysis on the NPV
Explicit cost-benefit of the strategic claims
required_conditions: Applies when a project's NPV is negative but management claims strategic benefits justify it.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — NPV decision rule / real-options theory
title: NPV negative but strategic benefits claimed

alternative_explanations: Projects differ greatly in scale (IRR is a percentage, NPV is absolute).
Cash-flow timing differences favour the earlier-returning project under IRR.
The IRR reinvestment assumption is unrealistic for this business.
One project's cash flows are less certain than the other's.
info_needed: Project sizes and cash-flow timing profiles
The cost of capital used for NPV
Realistic reinvestment opportunities for interim cash flows
Whether projects are truly mutually exclusive
interpretation: The two methods disagree, usually because of differences in project scale or cash-flow timing, or the reinvestment assumption buried in IRR. NPV at the cost of capital is the theoretically superior rule.
recommended_analysis: NPV at the cost of capital for both projects
Incremental IRR on the difference in cash flows
required_conditions: Applies when IRR ranks mutually exclusive projects differently from NPV.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — capital appraisal theory (reinvestment assumption)
title: IRR vs NPV conflict on mutually exclusive projects

alternative_explanations: The in-house cost includes allocated overhead that would not actually be saved.
The quote is a loss-leader or excludes hidden costs (transport, quality control).
Quality, lead time or reliability differences outweigh the price gap.
In-house production protects a strategic capability.
info_needed: Avoidable vs unavoidable cost split for in-house production
Full landed cost of the supplier quote (transport, duties, QC)
Alternative use and value of released capacity
Supplier reliability, quality record and contract terms
interpretation: Outsourcing may save money, but only relevant (avoidable) costs count. Allocated fixed overhead that will not disappear must be ignored, and the value of released capacity must be included.
required_conditions: Applies when an external supplier quotes below the apparent in-house cost.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — relevant costing principles
title: Make-or-buy signal: supplier quote below in-house cost

alternative_explanations: Spare capacity may be temporary; the order could displace future full-price sales.
The low price could leak to existing customers and erode normal pricing.
The order may carry hidden costs (customisation, overtime, penalties).
Accepting sets a precedent the customer will exploit.
info_needed: Spare capacity position and its expected duration
Variable cost per unit and any incremental fixed costs
Whether any regular sales would be displaced
Customer relationship and price-confidentiality safeguards
interpretation: The order should be judged on incremental profit: special price vs incremental (relevant) costs, including any contribution lost from displaced regular sales. Sunk and unavoidable fixed costs are irrelevant.
required_conditions: Applies when a one-off order is offered at a price below normal selling price.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — incremental analysis
title: Special order opportunity: one-off order at a special price

alternative_explanations: The bottleneck is short-term (breakdown, absence) rather than structural.
Demand, not the resource, is the real constraint for some products.
The constraint could be eased cheaply (overtime, minor investment).
Multiple constraints bind at once, needing fuller optimisation.
info_needed: Contribution per unit and limiting-factor usage per product
Maximum demand per product
Cost of easing the constraint
Whether other resources also bind
interpretation: With one binding constraint, profit is maximised by ranking products on contribution per unit of the limiting factor -- not on contribution per unit of product.
recommended_analysis: Optimal product mix with demand limits
required_conditions: Applies when a single scarce resource (machine hours, labour, material) limits production.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — limiting-factor / throughput analysis
title: Limiting factor: a scarce resource constrains output

alternative_explanations: The competitor's cut is a short promotion, not a structural move.
The competitor has a genuine cost advantage the business cannot match.
Customers value the business's differentiation more than price.
The cut targets a segment the business does not serve.
info_needed: Own variable cost and breakeven at candidate prices
Price elasticity and customer switching behaviour
Competitor cost position and staying power
Differentiation and non-price competitive strengths
interpretation: Matching the cut is not automatic. The right response depends on cost position, differentiation, and how customers actually choose -- a price war destroys margin for everyone.
recommended_analysis: Contribution impact of matching vs holding price
required_conditions: Applies when a competitor cuts prices and the business must respond.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — pricing theory
title: Pricing pressure: competitor has cut prices

alternative_explanations: A natural hedge exists (inflows and outflows in the same currency).
Prices can be passed through to customers (pricing power).
The exposure is short-term and immaterial in size.
Volatility is high but the trend consistently favours the business.
info_needed: Currency split, amounts and timing of exposed cash flows
Natural hedges already in place
Costs of forwards, options and other hedges
Ability to invoice in home currency or pass through prices
interpretation: Currency moves can wipe out margins on foreign transactions. The exposure should be quantified (amount, currency, timing) and a hedging or pricing response chosen deliberately.
recommended_analysis: Exposure quantification by currency and date
required_conditions: Applies when the business has material foreign-currency cash flows and exchange rates are volatile.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — foreign-exchange risk management theory
title: Foreign-exchange exposure with high currency volatility

alternative_explanations: Rate rises are expected to reverse quickly.
The business's income also rises with rates (natural offset).
Debt can be repaid or refinanced on fixed terms cheaply.
Covenant headroom is large enough to absorb the rise.
info_needed: Debt repricing schedule and sensitivity to a 1% rise
Covenant terms and headroom
Cost of fixing rates (swaps, caps, fixed refinancing)
Forecast cash flows under higher rates
interpretation: Debt servicing costs will rise automatically, squeezing profit and cash flow and potentially breaching covenants. The exposure should be measured and managed.
recommended_analysis: Interest-rate sensitivity of profit and cash flow
Hedge comparison (swap vs cap vs fixed refinancing)
required_conditions: Applies when the business carries floating-rate debt and interest rates are rising.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — interest-rate risk management theory
title: Interest-rate exposure: floating-rate debt as rates rise

alternative_explanations: A seasonal dip that reverses with the trading cycle.
Timing of a large receipt just after the period-end.
Strong undrawn facilities that the ratio does not show.
A planned, funded investment temporarily depressing cash.
info_needed: Short-term cash flow forecast (13-week view)
Undrawn borrowing facilities and their conditions
Aged payables and creditor pressure
Quality and realisability of current assets
interpretation: Short-term liabilities exceed short-term assets and cash is draining: the business may struggle to pay its bills as they fall due. This is urgent regardless of reported profit.
recommended_analysis: Cash flow forecast and funding gap
required_conditions: Applies when the current ratio is below 1.0 and cash balances are falling.
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — liquidity management theory
title: Liquidity crunch: current ratio below 1 and cash falling
Overtrading: rapid sales growth funded by stretching creditors
required_conditions: Applies when revenue is growing fast while payable days lengthen and short-term borrowing rises.
interpretation: The business is growing faster than its capital base can support: working capital is funded by delaying suppliers and borrowing short-term. This is overtrading -- profitable on paper but fragile, and it can collapse suddenly if credit is withdrawn.
alternative_explanations: A planned, funded expansion where the funding is already arranged.
Seasonal working-capital needs that reverse after the peak.
A one-off large contract distorting the trends.
Suppliers voluntarily offering longer terms as a relationship benefit.
info_needed: Cash conversion cycle trend
Ageing of payables and creditor pressure signs
Short-term facility limits and utilisation
Forecast funding gap under continued growth
recommended_analysis: Cash conversion cycle and funding-gap analysis
Sensitivity of cash to growth assumptions
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — overtrading literature

title: Dividend vs retention tension: payout pressure alongside investment needs
required_conditions: Applies when shareholders expect dividends but the business also has attractive investment opportunities needing funds.
interpretation: Cash paid out cannot fund growth. The choice signals to the market: cutting dividends may depress the share price, but over-distributing starves value-creating investment and may force expensive external finance.
alternative_explanations: The investment opportunities are weaker than claimed.
Dividend expectations are assumed, not actually expressed by shareholders.
External finance is cheap and readily available, easing the tension.
A stable dividend is needed for signalling in this market.
info_needed: Distributable profits and dividend cover
Capex pipeline with expected returns
Cost and availability of external finance
Shareholder composition and expectations
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — dividend policy theory

title: Rights issue: dilution and pricing effects of the fundraising
required_conditions: Applies when the business proposes a rights issue to existing shareholders.
interpretation: Existing shareholders face dilution unless they take up their rights; the theoretical ex-rights price (TERP) sets the benchmark for whether the terms are fair, and the discount depth affects take-up.
alternative_explanations: Debt finance may be cheaper or less dilutive.
The discount is small and the issue is effectively at market price.
Major shareholders have already committed to take up their rights.
info_needed: Rights terms (ratio, subscription price) and TERP calculation
Use of proceeds and expected return on the funds raised
Effect on EPS, gearing and control
Underwriting arrangements and costs
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — rights-issue mechanics

title: M&A synergy claims: promised benefits may not materialise
required_conditions: Applies when an acquisition case rests on synergy benefits (cost savings, revenue uplift).
interpretation: Synergies are easy to promise and hard to deliver: integration costs, culture clashes and customer losses routinely erode them. The premium paid must be justified by synergies that survive scrutiny, or the acquirer's shareholders lose.
alternative_explanations: The acquirer has a strong, evidenced integration track record.
Synergies are cost-based and largely within management's control.
The target is genuinely undervalued on a standalone basis.
info_needed: Synergy sources itemised (cost vs revenue) with timing
Integration costs and risks
Due-diligence findings on the target
Walk-away price based on standalone value
recommended_analysis: DCF of synergies vs premium paid
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — M&A valuation theory

title: Ethical red flag: pressure or opportunity to act unethically
required_conditions: Applies when facts suggest pressure to misstate, conceal, or bypass ethical/professional standards.
interpretation: This is not a technical optimisation problem: integrity and objectivity come first. Apply a structured ethical decision model, consider all affected stakeholders, and escalate through proper channels rather than acting alone.
alternative_explanations: A genuine error or misunderstanding, not intentional wrongdoing.
Commercial pressure being misread as unethical pressure.
Adequate safeguards already exist and are working.
info_needed: Full facts: who, what, when, and documentary evidence
Applicable code of ethics and professional standards
Available safeguards and escalation/whistleblowing channels
Stakeholders affected and how
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — professional ethics principles

title: Data/systems inadequacy: systems cannot support the decision
required_conditions: Applies when manual or technology-based systems and controls are inadequate for reliable data.
interpretation: Decisions built on unreliable data are unreliable. Fix the data and control foundation -- or explicitly qualify every conclusion -- before committing resources on the back of these numbers.
alternative_explanations: A training/usage gap rather than a system capability gap.
Controls exist but are not operated consistently.
The inadequacy affects only non-critical data.
info_needed: Specific system/control gaps and their impact on data quality
Cost and timeline of remediation options
Compensating manual controls in the interim
Data-quality testing results
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — internal control theory

title: Technology disruption threat to the business model
required_conditions: Applies when a technology threatens to substitute the product, service or channel.
interpretation: Disruption can strand assets and collapse margins faster than forecasts assume. The response ranges from adopting the technology to pivoting the business model -- but denial is the costliest option.
alternative_explanations: Hype: the technology is immature or uneconomic at scale.
The business's relationships, brand or regulation protect it.
The technology complements rather than substitutes the offering.
info_needed: Technology adoption rates and cost curves
Which customer jobs the technology does better
Own R&D and partnership options
Asset stranding exposure
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — innovation/disruption literature

title: New entrant competition threatening market position
required_conditions: Applies when a new competitor enters or credibly threatens to enter the market.
interpretation: Entry pressure squeezes prices and market share. The defence depends on barriers to entry (scale, brand, switching costs, regulation) and on whether the entrant targets the core or a niche.
alternative_explanations: The entrant targets a niche the business does not serve.
Barriers to entry are high and the threat is not credible.
The entrant may become an acquisition or partnership opportunity.
info_needed: Entrant's resources, pricing and target segment
Barriers to entry and their durability
Own cost position vs the entrant
Customer switching costs and loyalty
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — competitive strategy (Porter)

title: Supplier power: concentrated supply base creates dependency
required_conditions: Applies when a small number of suppliers account for a large share of inputs.
interpretation: Powerful suppliers can raise prices, dictate terms or disrupt supply. Single-sourcing may look efficient until the supplier fails or reprices -- resilience has a cost worth paying.
alternative_explanations: A strong, long-term partnership with aligned incentives.
Switching costs are low in practice despite concentration.
The supplier depends on the business as much as vice versa.
info_needed: Share of spend per supplier and contract terms
Alternative suppliers and switching costs
Total cost of dual-sourcing vs single-sourcing
Supplier financial health
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — supply-chain risk

title: Customer concentration: over-dependence on a key customer
required_conditions: Applies when the largest customer accounts for more than 30% of revenue.
interpretation: Losing one customer would remove over 30% of revenue -- a severe concentration risk. The customer also gains bargaining power over price and terms.
alternative_explanations: A secure long-term contract with the customer.
A genuine strategic partnership, not a transactional dependency.
The concentration is temporary (e.g. one large project).
info_needed: Contract terms, duration and renewal risk
Customer profitability after servicing costs
Pipeline for diversifying the customer base
Credit exposure to the customer
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — credit-risk management

title: Project cost overrun: actual costs materially above budget
required_conditions: Applies when a project's costs are running materially over budget.
interpretation: The overrun must be diagnosed: scope change, bad estimating, inefficiency or inflation each demand a different response. The forecast at completion -- not just the variance to date -- drives the decision to continue, re-scope or stop.
alternative_explanations: Approved scope changes that the budget was never updated for.
Front-loaded costs that will reverse later in the project.
Inflation or FX movements outside the team's control.
info_needed: Earned-value / progress vs spend data
Change log: approved vs unapproved scope changes
Revised forecast at completion
Root causes by cost category
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — project control concepts

title: High sensitivity: small assumption changes flip the decision
required_conditions: Applies when the appraisal outcome is highly sensitive to one or more key variables.
interpretation: The decision rests on a knife-edge: small, plausible moves in a key variable change the recommendation. Either gather better data on that variable, build in flexibility, or require a bigger margin of safety.
alternative_explanations: The base case is deliberately conservative, so sensitivity overstates risk.
Mitigants exist (hedges, flexible contracts) that the model ignores.
The sensitive variable is actually well understood and stable.
info_needed: Ranges and likelihoods for the sensitive variables
Breakeven values of each key variable
Available mitigants and their costs
Quality of the underlying estimates
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — risk and sensitivity analysis

title: Revenue growth without profit growth
required_conditions: Applies when revenue is growing but operating profit is falling.
interpretation: Growth is value-destroying at the margin: each extra unit of sales adds cost faster than revenue. Common causes are discounting to buy volume, rising input costs, or an adverse mix shift.
alternative_explanations: Deliberate investment phase (marketing, capacity) ahead of returns.
One-off costs depressing this period's profit.
Growth in a new, initially low-margin segment.
info_needed: Price, volume and mix effects on revenue
Cost behaviour: which costs grew faster than sales and why
Segment-level profitability
Whether discounting drove the volume
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — cost-volume-profit analysis

title: Profit/cash divergence: profit up, operating cash flow down
required_conditions: Applies when reported profit is rising but operating cash flow is falling.
interpretation: Earnings quality is suspect: profit is increasingly made of accruals and working-capital absorption rather than cash. Persistent divergence can signal aggressive recognition or simply a business consuming cash to grow.
alternative_explanations: Working-capital investment for genuine growth.
Timing differences that will reverse next period.
Large non-cash charges (e.g. depreciation on new investment).
info_needed: Operating cash flow to profit reconciliation
Accruals and working-capital movements detail
Revenue recognition policies and any changes
Aged receivables and inventory
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — earnings-quality literature

title: Operating-leverage risk: high fixed costs meet volatile demand
required_conditions: Applies when fixed costs are a high share of total costs and demand is volatile.
interpretation: High operating leverage turns demand swings into large profit swings: good in booms, dangerous in downturns. The breakeven point sits high, so even modest volume shortfalls create losses.
alternative_explanations: Fixed costs are committed but demand volatility is overstated.
Pricing power allows margins to absorb volume swings.
Costs can be flexed quickly (outsourcing, variable contracts).
info_needed: Fixed vs variable cost split
Breakeven volume vs demand scenarios
Demand volatility history and drivers
Options to variabilise costs
rule_source: Authored deterministic rule — operating leverage theory
